messages.subject: Variable Transformation and Response Curve
messages.subject_clean: Variable Transformation and Response Curve
messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked users,

I am using unmarked to fit single-species single season occupancy model.
Before fitting tne model, I examined the potential non-linear relationship between occupancy probability and each occupancy covariate by constructing a series of single-variable models. For each occupancy covariate (5 covariates : s2, s3, s4, s6, s7), we selected from among its original, log-transformed, and quadratic forms, and used the one with the smallest Akaike’s Information Criteria or AIC in later analyses.

#  examine the potential non-linear relationship
normal <- occu(~1~ s1,  data=pred, control=list(maxit=1000))
  log    <- occu( ~1~ log(s1+1)  ,    data= pred  , control=list(maxit=1000))
  sqr    <- occu ~1~ s1+I(s1^2)   , data= pred    , control=list(maxit=1000))

modList <- fitList(normal = normal, log = log, sqr = sqr)
modSel(modList)

The output showed that original form is the best for covariate s2, s3, s4 and s7. And the quadratic form is the best for s6 with lowest AIC:

nPars AIC delta AICwt cumltvWt sqr 4 959.86 0.00 0.493 0.49 log 3 959.91 0.05 0.480 0.97 normal 3 965.67 5.81 0.027 1.00

So I built the following occupancy model:

predNT <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, siteCovs=s, obsCovs=obsCovs)
pred <- occu(~1~ s2 + s3 + s4 + s6 + I(s6^2) + s7), data = predNT, control = list(maxit = 1000))

And then plotted the response curves based on the occupancy model:

# 2 :
pred <- occu(as.formula(paste(WindBest, "s2 + s3 + s4 + s6 + I(s6^2) + s7")), data = predNT)
newDats2 <- data.frame(s2 = seq(min(s$s2), max(s$s2), length=100),
                       s3 = mean(s$s3), s4 = mean(s$s4), s5 = mean(s$s5), s6 = mean(s$s6),
                       s7 = mean(s$s7), s8 = mean(s$s8), s9 = mean(s$s9), s10 = mean(s$s10), s1 = mean(s$s1))
Epreds2 <- as.data.frame(predict(pred, newdata=newDats2, type="state"))
with(Epreds2, {
  s2 <- newDats2$s2
  plot(s2, Predicted, xlab='s2', ylab="Occupancy probability",
       pch=16, cex.lab=1, ylim=c(0,1),type="l", lwd=2)
  lines(s2, Predicted-SE, lty=3)
  lines(s2, Predicted+SE, lty=3)
})

# 3 :
pred <- occu(as.formula(paste(WindBest, "s2 + s3 + s4 + s6 + I(s6^2) + s7")), data = predNT, control = list(maxit = 1000))
newDats3 <- data.frame(s3 = seq(min(s$s3), max(s$s3), length=100),
                       s2 = mean(s$s2), s4 = mean(s$s4), s5 = mean(s$s5), s6 = mean(s$s6),
                       s7 = mean(s$s7), s8 = mean(s$s8), s9 = mean(s$s9), s10 = mean(s$s10), s1 = mean(s$s1))
Epreds3 <- as.data.frame(predict(pred, newdata=newDats3, type="state"))
with(Epreds3, {
  s3 <- newDats3$s3
  plot(s3, Predicted, xlab='s3', ylab="Occupancy probability",
       pch=16, cex.lab=1, ylim=c(0,1),type="l", lwd=2)
  lines(s3, Predicted-SE, lty=3)
  lines(s3, Predicted+SE, lty=3)
})

# 4 :
pred <- occu(as.formula(paste(WindBest, "s2 + s3 + s4 + s6 + I(s6^2) + s7")), data = predNT, control = list(maxit = 1000))
newDats4 <- data.frame(s4 = seq(min(s$s4), max(s$s4), length=100),
                       s2 = mean(s$s2), s3 = mean(s$s3), s5 = mean(s$s5), s6 = mean(s$s6),
                       s7 = mean(s$s7), s8 = mean(s$s8), s9 = mean(s$s9), s10 = mean(s$s10), s1 = mean(s$s1))
Epreds4 <- as.data.frame(predict(pred, newdata=newDats4, type="state"))
with(Epreds4, {
  s4 <- newDats4$s4
  plot(s4, Predicted, xlab='s4', ylab="Occupancy probability",
       pch=16, cex.lab=1, ylim=c(0,1),type="l", lwd=2)
  lines(s4, Predicted-SE, lty=3)
  lines(s4, Predicted+SE, lty=3)
})

# 6:
pred <- occu(as.formula(paste(WindBest, "s2 + s3 + s4 + s6 + I(s6^2) + s7")), data = predNT)
newDats6 <- data.frame(s6 = seq(min(s$s6), max(s$s6), length=100),
                       s2 = mean(s$s2), s3 = mean(s$s3), s4 = mean(s$s4), s5 = mean(s$s5),
                       s7 = mean(s$s7), s8 = mean(s$s8), s9 = mean(s$s9), s10 = mean(s$s10), s1 = mean(s$s1))
Epreds6 <- as.data.frame(predict(pred, newdata=newDats6, type="state"))
with(Epreds6, {
  s6 <- newDats6$s6
  plot(s6, Predicted, xlab='s6', ylab="Occupancy probability",
       pch=16, cex.lab=1, ylim=c(0,1),type="l", lwd=2)
  lines(s6, Predicted-SE, lty=3)
  lines(s6, Predicted+SE, lty=3)
})

# 7:
pred <- occu(as.formula(paste(WindBest, "s2 + s3 + s4 + s6 + I(s6^2) + s7")), data = predNT)
newDats7 <- data.frame(s7 = seq(min(s$s7), max(s$s7), length=100),
                       s2 = mean(s$s2), s3 = mean(s$s3), s4 = mean(s$s4), s5 = mean(s$s5),
                       s6 = mean(s$s6), s8 = mean(s$s8), s9 = mean(s$s9), s10 = mean(s$s10), s1 = mean(s$s1))
Epreds7 <- as.data.frame(predict(pred, newdata=newDats7, type="state"))
with(Epreds7, {
  s7 <- newDats7$s7
  plot(s7, Predicted, xlab='s7', ylab="Occupancy probability",
       pch=16, cex.lab=1, ylim=c(0,1),type="l", lwd=2)
  lines(s7, Predicted-SE, lty=3)
  lines(s7, Predicted+SE, lty=3)
})

However, the response curves are very flat and weird. I've had the same problem many times before. When the model is coupled with the I(s^2) term, the response curve usually behaves abnormally flat, usually in the vicinity of 0 or 1.

I was wondering how to correctly add the I(s^2) term to the model and plot the response curve correctly?

I look forward to your help and replies. Thank you very much!

messages.body_plain:
Some suggestions -

Double check the pasted together formulas for accuracy, converting character to formula can lead to some unexpected behavior.

More importantly, what do the parameter estimates from these 'final' models look like? My guess is there are some parameter estimates with very large (>5) absolute values or very large standard errors. This can lead to strange figures like the ones you have. This indicates some kind of problem with the model such as optimization issues, separation, etc. and I would not use the output of such a model. Unfortunately looking solely at AIC scores will not avoid this problem as it is not uncommon for a "top-ranked" model to have these kinds of issues.The reason is usually specifying a model that is too complex relative to the available data.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeffrey and Marc,

Sorry it has been a while! Thank you all for your input. It was helpful for leading me in the right direction. I ended up doing a model for scats+cameras with only the method as a covariate, holding occupancy constant. There I can directly look at probability of detection based on survey method. I also have separate models for scat detection and camera detection that include covariates associated with each survey methods.

Thank you again!

Marwa

On Thursday, September 19, 2024 at 3:58:00 AM UTC-7 Marwa M wrote:
> Hi All,
>
> I am a graduate student looking for some help. I am studying the Sierra Nevada red fox in the Oregon Cascades. The species is elusive and has a low abundance, making them hard to detect. I set camera traps using a random stratified sampling design, and did scat surveys, when going to and from the camera stations (~2 surveys/sampling period at different times but across the same space). Because I did not always have cameras where I was surveying for scats, how do you think I can integrate these 2 methods into one model to compare detection probabilities (effectiveness) of each method?
>
> Eventually, I hope to combine my detections from these two methods to inform my single species occupancy models.
>
> I have looked into Nichols (2008) but am unsure if this model would work considering the methods I used were not done in the same location. Is there any way, I can integrate these two methods into one model and compare their detection probabilities? Any examples you can point me towards?
>
> Thanks for your help!
>
> Marwa

Il giorno giovedì 31 ottobre 2024 alle 19:53:21 UTC+1 Kery Marc ha scritto:
> Dear Walter,
>
> if you want such time-varying covariates in the abundance part of your model, then you cannot make the closure assumption for abundance over the same duration ---- since a time-varying covariate cannot affect abundance if the latter is constant. Thus, you will then need a model that allows N to vary over time. In unmarked, this is either the dynamic N-mix (or Dail-Madsen) model, or else you 'stack' your data in annual blocks (for 'year' read any other time period within which you assume closure), add a factor that indexes the year and then fit an Nmix model with year as a factor in both abundance and detection, and with a random site effect in abundance, to avoid committing the sin of pseudoreplication.
>
> Best regards  — Marc
>

messages.subject: New Applied Statistical Modeling book is out !
messages.subject_clean: New Applied Statistical Modeling book is out !
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

We have written a new stats textbook entitled  Applied Statistical Modelling for Ecologists – A practical guide to Bayesian and likelihood inference using R, JAGS, NIMBLE, Stan and TMB. The new ASM book provides a gentle introduction to the essential models of applied statistics: linear models, generalized linear models, mixed and hierarchical models. In addition, it introduces integrated models, which have become a mega-trend in statistical ecology during the last 30 years. All models are fit with both a likelihood and a Bayesian approach, using several powerful software packages widely used in research publications: JAGS, NIMBLE, Stan, and TMB. In addition, the foundational method of maximum likelihood is explained in a manner that ecologists can really understand, and every model is also fit by numerical maximization of a custom-written likelihood function in R. Finally, the ASM book contains a comprehensive chapter on model building, checking and selection, all of which topics that are challenging for budding ecological modelers. There is a companion R package ASMbook, which is available on CRAN.

The ASM book is the successor of the widely used  Introduction to WinBUGS for Ecologists (Kéry, Academic Press, 2010). Like its parent, it is extremely effective for both classroom use and self-study, allowing students and researchers alike to quickly learn, understand, and carry out a very wide range of statistical modelling tasks. But in addition, it can be used to learn statistical modeling using a wide range of cutting-edge model-fitting engines, and with Bayesian and likelihood inference alike.

A detailed Table of Contents of the ASM book is attached. For much more information, also about the different target audiences, modes of usage of the book, and tips for instructors and students, please have a look at the book website (here <https://www.elsevier.com/books-and-journals/book-companion/9780443137150>). The website also contains all code for free download, as well as a free bonus chapter on the binomial N-mixture model. That chapter demonstrates the use for model fitting of the R packages unmarked and  ubms, and of the software JAGS, NIMBLE, Stan and TMB, as well as of the “do-it-yourself maximum likelihood method”, and gives a flavour of the spirit in which we wrote the ASM book.

Best regards ---- Marc & Ken

messages.subject: GOF biased to amount of detections/observations?
messages.subject_clean: GOF biased to amount of detections/observations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to link the abundances of some forest bird species with the structure parameters of forests in Catalonia (Spain). As the abundances data come from a distance sampling method survey, I used the gdistsamp function to fit the models for each species and the parboot function to check if they were a good fit.

I ran the same model for 43 different species, with detections of those that were from 100 to 3500 for quite generalists and common species. The model is the same for all species, as I want to see how they compare in estimate values sizes to check the ones that are more sensitive to the forest structure parameters. I am aware that this arises problems as the model won't be too good for some of them. However, my main issue now is that, after running the parboot function for each and every 43 species models (Negative Binomial distribution as with Poisson most showed significant overdispersion),  25 species pass the Goodness of Fit tests while the rest do not. However, I realized now that almost all of those that did not pass, were the ones that had more than 1400 observations, so I am concerned that the test is biased: for species with lower numbers of observations, the model may pass the GOF test more easily, not because it’s a "better" model, but because there isn’t enough data to detect any issues with the fit. And with more observations, models have a harder time "passing" these tests because even small discrepancies between the model and the data become statistically significant.

I am adding a table for you to see the outputs of the GOF and the observations of each species (there are a full 5057 different sites in my data) and a example of a model for a species:

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have two questions about the occuMulti function for Rota multi-species occupancy model in unmarked package.

First, whether the same occupancy variables can be added to the first-order and second-order (or higher order) parts of the model?
For example. there are three species of A, B and C. Both their spatial occupancy (utilization) and interspecific interactions might be potientially affected by elevation. So, can we use the elevation to explain their spatial occupancy and interactions simultaneously. Just like:

stateformulas <- c("~elevation","~elevation","~elevation","~elevation","~elevation","~elevation","elevation")

What I wondered was, if their spatial occupancys were already explained by elevation, could their interspecific relationships not also be explained by elevation?

If that's the case, then:

stateformulas <- c("~elevation","~elevation","~elevation","~1","~1","~1","1")

or

stateformulas <- c("~1","~1","~1","~elevation","~elevation","~elevation","elevation")

Second, how to get the SE and 95%CI when estimating the species interaction factor (SIF) using occuMulti function?

We can get the estimations of  marginal probability of occupancy for species A(ψA) and B(ψB) and the SEs using the code:

ψA <- predict(Multimod, type="state", species="A")
ψB <- predict(Multimod, type="state", species="B")

We can also estimate the occpuancy probability of co-occurrence of A and B(ψAB) and the SE using the code:

ψAB <- predict(Multimod, type="state", species=c('A','B'))

So, using the formula SIF = ψAB/(ψA × ψB) (Mackenzie et al., 2004), we can their SIF estimations, but how to calculate the the SE and 95%CI  for their SIFs?

Any tips would be greatly appreciated! Thanks in advance!

Zhilin Li

messages.subject: Re: Whether the same occupancy variables can be added to the first-order and second-order (or higher order) parts of the model
messages.subject_clean: Whether the same occupancy variables can be added to the first-order and second-order (or higher order) parts of the model
messages.body_plain:
Yes, you can use the same covariates in the first order and higher order terms. Keep in mind it will usually be significantly harder to get good estimates of coefficients for the interaction terms (e.g. requiring many more sites).

There isn't an easy way to get the uncertainty for the SIF. I guess one strategy would be to bootstrap it -

1. Using the estimated coefs and variance-covariance matrix, get a bunch of bootstrap samples of the coefs from a multivariate normal
2. For each bootstrap rep, use the sampled coef vector to calculate the marginal and co-occurrence probabilities (you'd have to do this manually using the math in the Rota paper)
3. Then calculate SIF for each rep yielding a distribution of SIFs, and SEs, etc

More importantly though I'm not sure if the SIF is a useful (or valid) metric for the Rota multispecies model, particularly with >2 species. You already have the estimates of the interaction terms which is a much more direct estimate of the strength of the interaction.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone! I’m a graduate student planning to conduct research on how climate affects mammal distribution across a large area. I’ll be using camera trap data collected from multiple locations within the area of interest (AOI) (different space and time), with data collection spanning different periods (2015–2020).

Originally, I planned to use single-species occupancy in relation to environmental and climate variables. However, given the varied data collection periods, climatic conditions may also differ across locations. For instance, the extreme forest fires in 2015 may have significantly impacted the climate that year.

My question is: Given the differences in climatic conditions in each period of camera trapping effort, how can I analyze all this data to produce a single distribution prediction? There may be inappropriate assumptions because climate is time-sensitive.

Are there alternative methods or models that could be effective for this kind of dataset?

Any insights or recommendations would be greatly appreciated!

messages.body_plain:
The code output is hard to read but ultimately, each element in the obsCovs list must be a matrix with identical dimensions to each species y matrix. For some reason you have a list of lists (which unmarked does not support). I guess this relates to your imputed datasets but I don't quite understand what your end goal is with that. Furthermore within each nested list, the matrices have 76 rows and 1 column, implying 76 sites and 1 replicate occasion. But to fit this model  as with regular occupancy models you need >1 replicate occasion. So I recommend checking your y-matrix dimensions and figuring out why the obs cov dimensions have only one column. Year and effort seem like site-level covariates, meaning they do not change across occasions. If so put them in your siteCovs. You will still be able to use them in your detection formula.

If you are having trouble building the unmarkedFrameOccuMulti I recommend reading ?unmarkedFrameOccuMulti again, running the examples, and then comparing the structure of the known 'good' unmarkedFrame outputs from the examples with the structure you are trying to create, in order to identify differences that could be causing these issues.

Ken

messages.subject: Analyzing detection & density dsing distsamp with multi-year count data
messages.subject_clean: Analyzing detection & density dsing distsamp with multi-year count data
messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked Community,

I am reaching out to seek your guidance on the best approach to analyze my multi-year dataset using the unmarked package, distsamp, given some of the challenges I’m currently facing. I have already incorporated some of the advice shared by Ken Kellner (a previous thread <https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/9F_i-LwwW-A/m/J-pDaI2xBQAJ>) but have encountered issues that I’m hoping to get more clarity on.

Study overview:

I am studying a single species of alpine breeding bird in California.

Data were collected over five years (2018-2022) using a double-observer approach. I served as the primary observer, with different (but consistent) secondary observers each year.

Surveys were conducted as single-visit counts at 216 sites, organized into blocks of 8 points spaced 250 meters apart. Not all sites were surveyed each year, but each was visited at least three times over the five years.

This model is meant to build in to spatial analysis where I plan to estimate habitat suitability and predict a distribution and population for the species.

Data structure & covariates:

Detection data: Count data from each survey point, with distances recorded to detected birds.

Det Covs in best models were: slope, time of day (quadratic), and snow (measured as % cover in 50m at site)

Static site covariates: Distance to cliffs, woody vegetation cover, slope.

Dynamic site covariate: Annual variation in snow cover measured as a percentage within a 50m radius and distance to the nearest snow patch and distance to nearest snow patch

Spatial structure:

I am analyzing sites (there are 216 sites within 27 blocks). Prior to accounting for imperfect detection with unmarked, I ran a glmm with a neg binom and best modes (based on AIC) had covariates distance to snow, cliffs and water, woody vegetation and ‘block’ as a random factor. blocks consistently had zero detections, which might indicate unsuitable habitat.

Current approach:

Based on the advice received and current package capabilities, I opted to use distsamp due to its compatibility with my count and distance sampling data, even though it does not directly accommodate double-observer data, nor does it allow me to have a negative binomial distribution, ZIP, or random factors.

I used parametric bootstrapping (parboot) to assess model fit, which indicated some overdispersion (c-hat values up to 2.14) → I have included GOF table at bottom of page

Detection probabilities and density estimates varied significantly between years. For example, detection probabilities were sometimes over 100%, and density estimates (km2) are incredibly low as well (possibly because I am using all the zeros - even at sites where the birds were never seen in 3-5 surveys over the course of 5 years → I have included a table with det probs and density estimates at bottom of this page

Current challenges:

Handling zero detections:

Many blocks consistently had zero detections across all years, possibly indicating unsuitable habitat (that is to say I am analyzing by ‘site’ and so there are a huge number of zeros

some of these zeros make sense and are at sites that are within a single ‘block’ (or basin along the transect we surveyed at sites 1-8) and are generally at the lower elevations of the transect (sites 1-8 in a basin were almost always rising in an elevational gradient.

some of these zeros are zeros at sites 1-8 in a basin every year surveyed (i.e. unsuitable habitat)

Should I exclude these zero-detection sites to improve density estimates or incorporate a site-level random effect for blocks (though distsamp does not support random effects)?

Relative Abundance vs. True Density:

Since I am using distsamp without double-observer adjustments, am I effectively estimating relative abundance rather than true density?

If so, would this approach still support creating reliable habitat suitability maps and distribution models?

Where we have zeros within a basin (all 8 sites), based on my experience, there is unsuitable habitats – this and the low densities and reliable detection. Would this be better to approach from a true density approach?

Integration of double-observer data:

I analyzed detection probabilities using MRDS for my double-observer data. My plan is to put these coefficients into my distamp model to improve detection estimates – though I am still unsure of exactly how

This species is clustered in low densities within occupied habitats; they are very easy to detect and are reliably in the same general location for long periods of time – which can be shown by the match of counts at each site between Obv1 and Obv2 – even when these observations are spaced out in time.

Is there a recommended method to integrate the detection estimates from MRDS into my current distsamp analysis?

Overdisperson (alternaitve pkgs…. gdistamp)

Giving my distribution is skewed and GOF results are overfitting slightly, I wanted to try an run my models with NB or ZIP distribution and/or bring in a random factor – this seems only possible if I switch to the gdistamp package.

If I use gdistamp, won’t I be violating the assumptions? These breeding birds can be considered a ‘closed popn’ (I think) as they are tied to the nest during the surveys – when they fledge, we stop surveys, so there is not temporary emigration.

And we are doing single site visits each year, even though the second observer lags behind the first observer by about 1hr this is due to logistics, safety and terrain of the alpine.

Specific questions:

Should I exclude sites that consistently had zero detections (within a block, which would involve identify sites that are nested in a single block of non-occupancy), or continue treating each site as independent?

Given my dataset, is distsamp still the best approach, or should I shift to another function like gdistamp for better integration of detection probabilities?

If integrating double-observer estimates is possible, how can I do so within the unmarked framework?

I greatly appreciate any advice or suggestions you can provide. I know this maybe a lot, and I am close to wrapping up this analysis and need help from the experts to take it across the finish line!

Please ask clarifying questions!

Here are the detection probability estimates for the best models of each year and their densities.

Here is are the results of the parboot GOF tests. Note the high chi-sq values.

> The code output is hard to read but ultimately, each element in the obsCovs list must be a matrix with identical dimensions to each species y matrix. For some reason you have a list of lists (which unmarked does not support). I guess this relates to your imputed datasets but I don't quite understand what your end goal is with that. Furthermore within each nested list, the matrices have 76 rows and 1 column, implying 76 sites and 1 replicate occasion. But to fit this model  as with regular occupancy models you need >1 replicate occasion. So I recommend checking your y-matrix dimensions and figuring out why the obs cov dimensions have only one column. Year and effort seem like site-level covariates, meaning they do not change across occasions. If so put them in your siteCovs. You will still be able to use them in your detection formula.
>

messages.subject: Results of GoF sensitive to number of occasions
messages.subject_clean: Results of GoF sensitive to number of occasions
messages.body_plain:
Hello unmarked Google group,

This is my first post as I am new to the group!

I am studying the distribution of coyotes in the Sonoran desert. Due to high naïve occupancy, I am using the Royle-Nichols model. My camera trap dataset corresponds to a single season of 82 trapping nights for 87 sites, resulting in 533 coyote captures.

I first ran the analysis keeping the 82 occasions. My global model has 7 covariates, which complies with the rule of one covariate per 30 captures:
occuRN(~effort + occ ~NDVI + Palm + Wat + SF + BTJ, CYT)

I then ran a MacKenzie & Bailey Goodness of fit test calling for:
mb.gof.test(RN.CYT_global2, nsim = 1000, plot.hist = TRUE, maxK = NULL).

The P-value (0.443) is fine, but the c-hat is very low (0.19392). Looking at the chi-square table, I noticed that most of the expected frequencies were pretty low, resulting in large chi-square values. The same phenomenon seemed to happen with simulated data sets, with wide quantile intervals.

Following recommendations found in group conversations, I then ran the model pooling 3 and 7 trapping nights together. On average, observed and expected frequencies increased, leading to lower values of chi-square. However, P-value and c-hat are very sensitive to pooling:

·        3 trapping nights: P-value = 0.071, c-hat = 1.83631

·        7 trapping nights: P-value = 0.826, c-hat = 0.69597

messages.subject: Looking for recommendations for analysis of small mammal data
messages.subject_clean: Looking for recommendations for analysis of small mammal data
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I was given a small mammal dataset to analyze and I've never analyzed this type of data. I'm wondering what an appropriate or good model would be.

Sampling details: 93 sites were sampled over 9 years (2014-2022). 8 - 12 plots were sampled per year and a given plot was sampled just once in the 9 years. At each site, 3 transects were sampled (in 3 directions, e.g., at 60, 180, and 270 degrees, from a plot center) and each transect had 10 - 20 trapping stations (varies from year to year) with a snap trap, a sherman trap, and a pitfall trap. Traps were checked 3 consecutive nights and they recorded the species trapped, or whether the trap was sprung, bait taken, open, or etc.

Constraints/questions: I need to do this analysis quickly (over about two days; thus posting here versus hierarchical modeling) and I just view this as exploratory. There aren't any particular questions with this data; I'd like to offer something about occupancy or abundance, site to site variability, and year to year variability. There's some year to year noise given different yearly effort/skill in species identification (e.g., shrew spp. in some years, versus identified to species level in others). Any suggestions on what to look at here would be welcome as well. I have one habitat covariate and a handful of detection covariates (date, weather, etc.). There are also some morphometrics for the small mammals such as weight, body length, etc.

Thanks in advance,
Valerie

messages.body_plain:
hi Valerie,
 I'm afraid that getting something done in a couple days will probably be a stretch since there seems to be a lot of aspects to your data. That said, if the individual animals were marked then this would be an ideal situation for a spatial capture-recapture model.   It's not clear if they were marked though.
 Was the sampling for each grid repeated on consecutive days?  Or were the traps set, checked, and then pulled?   If the latter, then this is probably best viewed as a logistic regression (or possibly Poisson regression depending on if detections are aggregated to sites).  Without replication you won't be able to fit occupancy or related models.

 Its curious that a new set of sites were surveyed in each year so that there are no replicate samples of any given site.  That's not a typical design and seems limiting from the standpoint of understanding animal population structure or dynamics.

 Sorry I can't give more specific advice at this point.
regards
andy

Hi Andy,

They had a code for 'recapture', but few captures were marked as such. Thus, I don't think they reliably tracked this. Traps were placed 15-m apart. Thank you for the occupancy model idea at the trap station level. I hadn't thought of that, but that might be the way to go! I could probably use the ubms package to allow me to include a random effect of plot. However, I can't wrap my head around how to accommodate the multiple trap types for each station, and to complicate that even more, this differed by year where in 2014-2017 each station had a pitfall, sherman and snap trap and from 2018-2022 snap traps were no longer used. Any thoughts here?

And, yes, agreed about the deficiency in the sampling design for looking at temporal variability. I plan to give them that feedback.

Thanks for your reply and help!
Valerie

Hi Valerie and Andy,

For a case where you were using multiple traps at the same site, if you're using an occupancy model, I might suggest using the multi-method AKA multi-scale model. I don't think multi-scale models are currently available in unmarked, but you could consider using PRESENCE or Mark. It sounds like if you surveyed different sites each year, it might make the most sense to run a separate occupancy model for each year? i'm not quite sure how to handle the multi-year aspect of the data as you've described it.

If you decide that a multi-scale model is the way to go, and need help implementing it PRESENCE or Mark, I'd be happy to help.

messages.body_plain:
hi Reed,
  the new unmarked function goccu will fit the multi-method type of models I believe.  Ken just added this over the summer, so check it out.  One thing I'm not sure about with Valerie's data is that the methods are not sampling independently. For example, there is probably a negative association between getting caught in a snap trap and getting caught in a live trap when population densities are low.  In this case maybe the multi-state occupancy models would be more suitable (occuMS I think).
regards
andy

On Fri, Nov 22, 2024 at 11:11 AM Reed Scott <rscot...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Valerie and Andy,
>
> For a case where you were using multiple traps at the same site, if you're using an occupancy model, I might suggest using the multi-method AKA multi-scale model. I don't think multi-scale models are currently available in unmarked, but you could consider using PRESENCE or Mark. It sounds like if you surveyed different sites each year, it might make the most sense to run a separate occupancy model for each year? i'm not quite sure how to handle the multi-year aspect of the data as you've described it.
>
> If you decide that a multi-scale model is the way to go, and need help implementing it PRESENCE or Mark, I'd be happy to help.
>
> On Fri, Nov 22, 2024 at 10:15 AM Valerie Steen <valeri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Andy,
> >
> > They had a code for 'recapture', but few captures were marked as such. Thus, I don't think they reliably tracked this. Traps were placed 15-m apart. Thank you for the occupancy model idea at the trap station level. I hadn't thought of that, but that might be the way to go! I could probably use the ubms package to allow me to include a random effect of plot. However, I can't wrap my head around how to accommodate the multiple trap types for each station, and to complicate that even more, this differed by year where in 2014-2017 each station had a pitfall, sherman and snap trap and from 2018-2022 snap traps were no longer used. Any thoughts here?
> >
> > And, yes, agreed about the deficiency in the sampling design for looking at temporal variability. I plan to give them that feedback.
> >
> > Thanks for your reply and help!
> > Valerie
> >
> > On Thu, Nov 21, 2024 at 3:57 PM Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > hi Valerie,
> > >  ok I missed the detail that the traps were run for 3 consecutive nights.... so then: were individuals marked?   If so then capture-recapture is the way to go.  If not then you could fit occupancy models perhaps using "traps" as sites.  (how far apart were the traps?).
> > >  There would be some spatial dependence to consider for neighboring traps perhaps.  At any rate a "basic occupancy" model could be made to run in relatively short order
> > >  (sorry for misreading your email and my errant initial response)
> > > regards
> > > andy
> > >
> > >
> > > On Thu, Nov 21, 2024 at 10:36 AM Valerie Steen <valeri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hello all,
> > > >
> > > > I was given a small mammal dataset to analyze and I've never analyzed this type of data. I'm wondering what an appropriate or good model would be.
> > > >
> > > > Sampling details: 93 sites were sampled over 9 years (2014-2022). 8 - 12 plots were sampled per year and a given plot was sampled just once in the 9 years. At each site, 3 transects were sampled (in 3 directions, e.g., at 60, 180, and 270 degrees, from a plot center) and each transect had 10 - 20 trapping stations (varies from year to year) with a snap trap, a sherman trap, and a pitfall trap. Traps were checked 3 consecutive nights and they recorded the species trapped, or whether the trap was sprung, bait taken, open, or etc.
> > > >
> > > > Constraints/questions: I need to do this analysis quickly (over about two days; thus posting here versus hierarchical modeling) and I just view this as exploratory. There aren't any particular questions with this data; I'd like to offer something about occupancy or abundance, site to site variability, and year to year variability. There's some year to year noise given different yearly effort/skill in species identification (e.g., shrew spp. in some years, versus identified to species level in others). Any suggestions on what to look at here would be welcome as well. I have one habitat covariate and a handful of detection covariates (date, weather, etc.). There are also some morphometrics for the small mammals such as weight, body length, etc.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks in advance,
> > > > Valerie
